Hout Bay Harbour - what now?

By: Liz Fish | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Whats the story: Two new Ministers – both DA- both with extremely difficult portfolios of the Department of Public Works and Department of Forestry Fisheries and Environment jointly responsible for the running of the harbours. They have been making bold statements and fresh promises to revitalise the Hout Bay harbour. This is an update on our 2022 story when Derek stood inside stripped buildings and then Minister of Public Works Patricia De Lille made promises - which are still on our website.
Hout Bay like Kalk Bay is one of the most visited tourists’ spots in Cape Town. Every weekend people cue to get a spot at Fish on the Rocks. The red tour bus stops outside the Hout Bay market and the place is pumping. Tourism is the big business in the Western Cape - so what's holding up this master development plan for Hout Bay harbour that's been on the cards for the last 15 years?


Summary:
DFFE Min George stated that the sunken wrecks must be lifted by the 16th June by the owners ,or the Department would do it and charge them. Sunken wrecks hamper the 3 main commercial fishing business - Tuna, Hake and Lobster. That date came and went and on 25th June another site visit – SAMSA are tasked with the job. The dry dock is working again, and Min. George of DFFE has established a working committee with local business and fishing business. Signage and painting within the harbour is underway and security contracts being negotiated. So there is definitely more transparency. BUT the people who work and make Hout Bay harbour what it is - are working under extremely tenuous circumstances. DPW won’t issue leases for more than a year and all maintenance and security is the tenants problem.


Further information:
Case Study 1 “Fish on the Rocks” nestled below Hangberg Fishing Village, on the far side of the Hout bay harbour, is a family business that’s history that goes back to the early 1900. Alfred Broderic at 83 still goes to work every day. He took over the business in the early 1980s with his beloved wife Najmuneesa, from her mother Habibchilwane. Initially Fish on the Rock was known as Snoekies- then it was a shed that dried snoek and fed the local fishermen at lunch time. It was the corner store and the only place with a telephone. Habibchilwane – Najmunessa mother and Shafika’s grandmother was the matriarch who cared for her poorer neighbours running a soup kitchen and supporting local school kids.
Alfred a Brit, landed in South Africa in the 60’s met and fell in love with Najmunessa – they had 3 children but living in a “mixed” marriage was difficult for the family. Shafika is the oldest daughter and will tell their story alongside her father Alfred. Sadly, Najimunessa died suddenly after a short illness two years ago. Alfred seems lost without her driving force but ensures he is at Fish on the Rocks every day and is keeping the business thriving so he can pass it on to his children. But how much longer can he hold on?
Alfred and Najmunesaa bought the business from Habibchilwane in 1988 owning 50/50 shares. They had a 20-year lease which came to an end 3 years ago and since then they have been given a yearly lease but it’s creating an enormous amount of stress and uncertainty. Alfred says when he attends the meetings with Government officials and local leaders he knows less than he did when he arrived. He wants to expand the premises, add more toilets, create better staff changerooms and toilets and protect his staff from the elements but without proper tenure he can’t afford to. They employ over 40 people from the local community.
Shafika – his eldest daughter, who strongly resembles her mother and Grandmother is rooted in this community and talks of her Great Grandfather walking over the dunes from Llandudno in 1896 when he was shipwrecked. He was Malaysian and his wife Indian. They settled in Hout Bay when there was nothing but fish and trees. Habibchilwane opened the corner Café in 1942 and raised her children a few streets from where Fish on the Rocks stands today
Fish on the Rocks grew from a shed with a bus gradually over the years and their Muslim clientele come from across Cape Town. They serve no alcohol, and their business is thriving- on the weekends there are cues of people and parking becomes a problem.
Case Study 2” Sean Walker, Managing Director, of Breakwater Products Pty Ltd, is competing on a global Tuna market and has fought hard to get accreditation South African albacore tuna pole and line fishery, certification from the globally recognised standard for sustainable fishing set by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)
But working conditions in the Hout Bay harbour make life extremely stressful. The Breakwater factory burnt down 8 years ago when the local community fought police over the death of a poacher. A petrol bomb on the roof of the factory destroyed Sean Walker packing and processing shed. Since then, he has been trying to rebuild but the Department of Public Works refuses to give him a lease.
He has met with Deon George and is part of the working group that the Minister established. The sucken wrecks are a major problem. The Tuna boats hardly have anywhere to birth to unload their catch which has to be landed and flown out the country within hours. The boat owners must pay for their own security – like Fish on the Rocks. But water and electricity outages are on going, and trying to run an ice factory is a nightmare. Petty theft is ongoing despite DFFE having a massive security contract which does nothing but guard the remaining bricks in the stripped building. Copper theft to a refrigeration unit last month cost R50 000 to replace. Sean is at breaking point. But last time he spoke out the police, fisheries inspectors and immigration police descended on him, he is unsure if its worth speaking his mind. But he wants to tell a positive story and is encouraged by the efforts Min.George is making but says DPW have been deadly quite since the visit in May.
3rd case Study “Peter Roeloffze- has the bigger picture. He owns the Urban Brewery just outside the harbour yet the DPW owns the buildings and is caught in the net of the development plans of the harbour. Peter invested R7 million and on the Brewery. He has met with Minister Dean Macpherson three times. The master plan is to develop Hout Bay harbour which Peter supports. But this is what holds all the business to ransom. This master plan has been on the table for over 15 years and when the long-term leases ran out, they all forced to sign one-year leases so if and when a developer is in place they able to go ahead. But this is hampering local businesspeople. And ontop of only getting a 1-year lease it doesn’t not cover any maintenance or security. So, the harbour stagnates and good business that employ 100s of locals can’t get ahead. Solar power, toilets for guests, improving access and growing the local economy are all throttled.



Extra Budget Items:
Extra shoot day to get cutaways on a weekend and Ministers additional interview as trying to get both Minister in the same week is an issue. Makes shooting sequentially difficult

Script:


VO1: Whittles “An air of gloom hangs over Cape Town’s Hout Bay harbour -
Breath
Alfred Broderick How do you plan something when there appears to be no future?
VO 2: Whittles “For the last 43 years the one thing Alfred Broderick was certain of – is hanging in the balance.
Alfred Broderick” It's like coming to the roundabout. do you go left. Right. Straight on. Or nowhere.
Upsound “ Arriving at the shop and greeting staff
VO 3 Whittles ” Now 83, he wonders how much longer his business will be around.

VO 4 Whittles “For the past 15 years, tenants like Alfred have been holding out for Hout Bay Harbour’s promised redevelopment. But, meeting after meeting, nothing happens.

VO4a Will the Government finally act for the people who depend on this harbour – or is something else being planned?”


Alfred Broderick:. We're were always ong term leases, …Our previous lease was for 22 years….the staff, the family, the grandchildren know what they're going to do for the next 22 years.
Govan Whittles: What, uh, when did that lease expire?
Alfred Broderick: About three years ago.
Govan Whittles: Why are they doing that?
Alfred Broderick: Communication is between nil and zero there is nothing. 0:07:11:21 No one can explain. And the more you try and find out, the less you find out. So now we're just living from going from year to year.

VO 5 Whittles: “Alfred’s family helps him run the shop — it’s their inheritance he fears is at risk.

His daughter Shafeeka describes a legacy going back to the early 1900’s.

Shafeeka Broderick : Well, it all started when my great grandfather had a boat that stranded on the Atlantic coast near Llandudno. And they walked over into these mountains, which was just forest at the time, and they began to set up life.

VO 6 Whittles“Her grandmother started the family business 58 years ago.

Shafeeka Broderic 00:00:47:00 my grandfather was a fisherman and my own father, who's English. He brought the concept of English fish and chips. And so there was all sorts of heritage coming together.

VO 7 Whittles” Alfred and his wife ran the shop for more than four decades – the heart and soul of the place, she died two years ago.
Govan Whittles:Do you feel a like a sense of responsibility that you have to preserve the legacy?

Alfred Broderic: Yes. You want to keep that legacy going. It's not a franchise, it’s just an existing building and its run naturally. The staff are local, we are local. We come to work within ten minutes walk. 00:18:52:09 It's not just for me. It's for the for the families, parents who work here

VO 8 Whittles: Broderick has no security of tenure. He owns his building — unlike most tenants — but the Government owns the prime land beneath it.
-Alfred Broderick ..you can't expand the business. You want to build extra toilets, we want to build another deck. …maintenance of the building is expensive. Being next to the sea. we want to commit ourselves here for another 50 years

VO 9 Whittles “Something doesn’t add up. No one in this harbour has secure tenure — only short leases, some month to month. A whole harbour left in limbo.”

Sean Walker “At the moment, we we all just work on a month to month, year to year basis, …
VO 10: Whittles“Sean Walker owns one of the major tuna processing factories and plays a central role in the tuna fleet operating from here.”
“Sean Walker“.It's it's it's a terribly stressful way to try and run a business and make it long term sustainable, for the business , for the economic viability of the business, for the sustainability of the jobs that we create. It's very stressful.
VO 11. Whittles: Tenants have been strung along since 2013 with promises of long term leases and a major redevelopment
Sean: The communication is that the leases are on hold …six months later, we get told that they're finalizing the leases in a months time. In fact its been the story for almost ten years
Link 39800 These concrete columns are all that is left of a fish processing facility that was burnt down years ago during a protest and the owners have never been able to secure a long term lease to rebuild it
Clip 9888 Sean Walker : 00:06:10:16 “Since 2018, we've basically been begging the department to allow us to rebuild this factory,the only way we can get value to that fish is through an efficient facility. And we've been working for since 2018, in a facility that is so radically inefficient and ineffective that it's impossible to make a profit.
VO 13 Whittles:” The Government owns everything up until the shoreline, much of which it has left to decay .
LINK UPSOUND Derek Watts “Just how do you take apart an entire factory over 13000 square meters in broad day light
VO14 Whittles “We last stood here in 2022 — when vandals had torn this entire area apart.”

Sean Walker “ 00:02:47:05 We don't understand how they can sit by and just allow this harbor to rot like it has. It doesn't make any sense, I'm sure that the intentions are there to resurrect it and and get it to see its potential, but that it can take this long to achieve. It's almost criminal
VO 15 Whittles: And the tenets carry the load. The only thing that changed is an expensive security contract to guard these destroyed buildings, paid for by the government. That hasn’t stopped the petty crime happening in plain sight"
Breath
VO 16 Whittles “The Department of Public Works oversees the harbour, and, after agreeing to meet us, Minister, Dean Macpherson, at last cut to the chase.”
Govan: So we know that 10 million was set aside for that spatial framework project in 2013, that the DG of the department in 2023 said that standardised leases would be finalised. As of right now, those leases are not in place. Why is that?

Min. Dean McPherson: The majority of leases actually have been concluded to give people security for a few years, but I think that's got to be looked at in the broader picture of what we want to do with this harbour.We think that there's the potential to create a VNA 2.0 here, which could attract between 1 billion and 1.5 billion USD worth of investment. Tens of thousands of jobs. But in order to be able to do that, we're going to have to have the flexibility to redevelop this. So of course if you gave people ten year leases, you're not going to be able to realize that plan.

VO 17 Whittles: This was news to Sean – he was told his business would be central to its future - are they just place holders while more attractive tenant opportunities come Governments way?

Sean Walker: Wow that is very surprising. If they told us 15 years ago that they're going to do that and they did it, then we'd all just make a plan, move on, but don't keep promising us that we're going to get leases, year after year after year and no leases, no security of tender It's just impossible to plan.

VO 18: Whittles “The V&A Waterfront, 20km away, is privately owned and is a mix of shops and hotels attracting over 25 million visitors a year. But rentals and berthing fees are exorbitant. A development like this could potentially destroy Hout Bay’s small businesses"

Peter Roeloffze ““This is the gate that we have widened all funded by the tenets here so its a safe entry for the tourist bus to come through here

VO 19 Whittles“ “Peter Roeloffze and his fellow tenants are working to boost tourism. He runs a brewery in a building housing several businesses — yet not one of them has a lease.”


Govan: Is a private owner holding the long lease. Good or bad for the businesses here?

Peter Roeloffze: I think it would be a good thing, as long as there are measures in place so that you don't start to get exorbitant rates, especially when you think of the local community, for instance in this building we have a section that we have ear marked which are community improvement where you have people doing charity work which we have said that area should be rent free. If you have a private person in, will they see it in the same light? I don’t know, will there be measures in place that's the questions we have got to ask 00:13:53:24 But must say under the guidance of Minister Macpherson, it has improved tremendously.

VO 20 Whittles : But Sean is wary
Clip 39888 00:17:18:20 -Sean Walker : I guess I get a little bit nervous when I hear the word private developer, because all that's going to do is push up the price of those opportunities …Somebody gets a fancy deal,....at somebody else's expense at the real entrepreneur's expense. And that just pushes up the price of the entrepreneur, which handicaps us further.
VO 21 Whittles”“For 15 years, these businesses have created jobs, fought crime, and tried to survive without security of tenure — all the while being told the new development was in their interests. But now it looms as a major threat.”
00:40:37:16 Govan:. So you expect people to take the one year lease, maintain their own buildings, pay for their own security while you find the private partner. And you think that's fair?



- Min. Dean McPherson: of course it's not, but we also suffer from budget cuts. I mean, if if we were to maintain every building that we have, I would need, you know, billions and billions more, which I don't get, which is why we are trying responsibility.And thats why we need to develop this to their benefit. You can't have a situation. Were we want to redevelop this entire precinct. And then a business is stopping all of that because they have a ten year lease.
VO 22 Whittles “The local fishing industry has effectively been pushed out of the V&A Waterfront, and Sean warns the same might happen in Hout Bay.”
Sean 00:09:13:21 - It's really beautiful. It's a jewel of Southern Africa. But the fishing industry has been sidelined…. more and more every year, the berthing spaces just get less and less and less as the shopping centers decide that they don't want noisy, smelly fishing boats near their operations and they just get pushed further and further away into no space at all.

VO 23 Whittles: "But McPherson, is confident the fishing industry will be accommodated

00:37:03:24 Min. Dean McPherson: so we want to make sure that the harbor is upgraded so that the fishing community and fishing businesses here are able to do much more and much better.


Govan: Can you guarantee that Fish on the Rocks, for example, won't be asked to move?

00:22:48:03 -Min. Dean McPherson: I can't guarantee that because if I did, I would then be setting unlawful demands on a, on a, on a, on a public process. And that would be a wrong for me to do so. But what I can say to every person is that every single person will be consulted, their needs will be looked into and, the best availability and best options will be presented to them.

VO24 Whittles It’s hard to see how protecting the current tenants squares with being unable to offer them any assurances
:41:44:07 - Min. Dean McPherson: I'm saying that we are working as quickly as we can to make this place better than what it is.
00:33:27:09 - 00:33:30:16 Govan: But can you give us a date? Will it take another 15 years?


Min. Dean McPherson "Definitely I won’t be here in 15 years time

Govan : Will it take another 5 years

Min. Dean McPherson In needs to be completed by the time I leave office. If I am still here in 4 years time, that has to be done.

VO25 Whittles: “Will it happen in Alfred Broderic’s lifetime? Will his family’s legacy survive — and will he finally see it in black and white?”

Shafeeka Broderick: Let communicate, lets collaborate and bring alive what is valuable to Hout Bay , what is valuable to the community, what is valuable in heart spirit and soul for everyone

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Whats the story: Two new Ministers – both DA- both with extremely difficult portfolios of the Department of Public Works and Department of Forestry Fisheries and Environment jointly responsible for the running of the harbours. They have been making bold statements and fresh promises to revitalise the Hout Bay harbour. This is an update on our 2022 story when Derek stood inside stripped buildings and then Minister of Public Works Patricia De Lille made promises - which are still on our website. Hout Bay like Kalk Bay is one of the most visited tourists’ spots in Cape Town. Every weekend people cue to get a spot at Fish on the Rocks. The red tour bus stops outside the Hout Bay market and the place is pumping. Tourism is the big business in the Western Cape - so what's holding up this master development plan for Hout Bay harbour that's been on the cards for the last 15 years?
metadata.Summary: DFFE Min George stated that the sunken wrecks must be lifted by the 16th June by the owners ,or the Department would do it and charge them. Sunken wrecks hamper the 3 main commercial fishing business - Tuna, Hake and Lobster. That date came and went and on 25th June another site visit – SAMSA are tasked with the job. The dry dock is working again, and Min. George of DFFE has established a working committee with local business and fishing business. Signage and painting within the harbour is underway and security contracts being negotiated. So there is definitely more transparency. BUT the people who work and make Hout Bay harbour what it is - are working under extremely tenuous circumstances. DPW won’t issue leases for more than a year and all maintenance and security is the tenants problem.
metadata.Further information: Case Study 1 “Fish on the Rocks” nestled below Hangberg Fishing Village, on the far side of the Hout bay harbour, is a family business that’s history that goes back to the early 1900. Alfred Broderic at 83 still goes to work every day. He took over the business in the early 1980s with his beloved wife Najmuneesa, from her mother Habibchilwane. Initially Fish on the Rock was known as Snoekies- then it was a shed that dried snoek and fed the local fishermen at lunch time. It was the corner store and the only place with a telephone. Habibchilwane – Najmunessa mother and Shafika’s grandmother was the matriarch who cared for her poorer neighbours running a soup kitchen and supporting local school kids. Alfred a Brit, landed in South Africa in the 60’s met and fell in love with Najmunessa – they had 3 children but living in a “mixed” marriage was difficult for the family. Shafika is the oldest daughter and will tell their story alongside her father Alfred. Sadly, Najimunessa died suddenly after a short illness two years ago. Alfred seems lost without her driving force but ensures he is at Fish on the Rocks every day and is keeping the business thriving so he can pass it on to his children. But how much longer can he hold on? Alfred and Najmunesaa bought the business from Habibchilwane in 1988 owning 50/50 shares. They had a 20-year lease which came to an end 3 years ago and since then they have been given a yearly lease but it’s creating an enormous amount of stress and uncertainty. Alfred says when he attends the meetings with Government officials and local leaders he knows less than he did when he arrived. He wants to expand the premises, add more toilets, create better staff changerooms and toilets and protect his staff from the elements but without proper tenure he can’t afford to. They employ over 40 people from the local community. Shafika – his eldest daughter, who strongly resembles her mother and Grandmother is rooted in this community and talks of her Great Grandfather walking over the dunes from Llandudno in 1896 when he was shipwrecked. He was Malaysian and his wife Indian. They settled in Hout Bay when there was nothing but fish and trees. Habibchilwane opened the corner Café in 1942 and raised her children a few streets from where Fish on the Rocks stands today Fish on the Rocks grew from a shed with a bus gradually over the years and their Muslim clientele come from across Cape Town. They serve no alcohol, and their business is thriving- on the weekends there are cues of people and parking becomes a problem. Case Study 2” Sean Walker, Managing Director, of Breakwater Products Pty Ltd, is competing on a global Tuna market and has fought hard to get accreditation South African albacore tuna pole and line fishery, certification from the globally recognised standard for sustainable fishing set by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) But working conditions in the Hout Bay harbour make life extremely stressful. The Breakwater factory burnt down 8 years ago when the local community fought police over the death of a poacher. A petrol bomb on the roof of the factory destroyed Sean Walker packing and processing shed. Since then, he has been trying to rebuild but the Department of Public Works refuses to give him a lease. He has met with Deon George and is part of the working group that the Minister established. The sucken wrecks are a major problem. The Tuna boats hardly have anywhere to birth to unload their catch which has to be landed and flown out the country within hours. The boat owners must pay for their own security – like Fish on the Rocks. But water and electricity outages are on going, and trying to run an ice factory is a nightmare. Petty theft is ongoing despite DFFE having a massive security contract which does nothing but guard the remaining bricks in the stripped building. Copper theft to a refrigeration unit last month cost R50 000 to replace. Sean is at breaking point. But last time he spoke out the police, fisheries inspectors and immigration police descended on him, he is unsure if its worth speaking his mind. But he wants to tell a positive story and is encouraged by the efforts Min.George is making but says DPW have been deadly quite since the visit in May. 3rd case Study “Peter Roeloffze- has the bigger picture. He owns the Urban Brewery just outside the harbour yet the DPW owns the buildings and is caught in the net of the development plans of the harbour. Peter invested R7 million and on the Brewery. He has met with Minister Dean Macpherson three times. The master plan is to develop Hout Bay harbour which Peter supports. But this is what holds all the business to ransom. This master plan has been on the table for over 15 years and when the long-term leases ran out, they all forced to sign one-year leases so if and when a developer is in place they able to go ahead. But this is hampering local businesspeople. And ontop of only getting a 1-year lease it doesn’t not cover any maintenance or security. So, the harbour stagnates and good business that employ 100s of locals can’t get ahead. Solar power, toilets for guests, improving access and growing the local economy are all throttled.
